### Comment 3: Additional Real-world applications with larger models

**Reviewer Comment:**

The real-world evaluation in Section 5.2 is limited to MicroDiffusion. It remains unclear how Ambient Dataloops scale to larger, widely used diffusion models (+ finetuning). For practical adoption, evidence on larger models would be important.

**Author Response:**

We agree with the reviewer that more evidence for larger models and real-world settings is always helpful, especially for practical adoption. For this, we use the state-of-the-art image-generation model Flux (12B) to "restore" ImageNet, i.e., to improve the quality of ImageNet images without compromising the diversity of the dataset. We provide examples from this "improved" ImageNet in Figure 6, and quantitative results in Tables 6 and 7, found in Appendix Section C of the revised paper.

These examples show that only the quality of the images improved, without altering what is actually depicted in the image. To actually quantify the improvement of quality on ImageNet, we use the CLIP-IQA metric. The results for the original ImageNet and the improved ImageNet are in Tables 6 and 7 in the paper, and also copied below for clarity:

**Table 6: CLIP-IQA Statistics**

| Dataset | Mean ± Std | Min | Max |
|---------|------------|-----|-----|
| Original ImageNet | 0.7251 ± 0.1572 | 0.0184 | 0.9959 |
| Flux-Restored | 0.7469 ± 0.1501 | 0.0265 | 0.9971 |

**Table 7: Pairwise Comparison Winrates**

| Dataset | Winrate Count and % |
|---------|---------------------|
| Original ImageNet wins | 37.82% |
| Flux-Restored wins | 62.17% |

These metrics, paired with our visuals, show that the quality of the dataset improved.

Moreover, we kindly point the reviewer towards Section 5.3 "De-Novo Protein Design" where we apply the Ambient Dataloops algorithm to a widely-used scientific application on a medium-sized 17M parameter model, which constitutes another real-world application.

### Weakness 4: Approximation of Noisy Clean Data by Noisy Corrupted Data

**Reviewer Comment:**

A crucial part of the paper is the approximation that the noisy distribution of the corrupted data almost coincides with the noisy distribution of clean data. The authors should investigate this approximation more in detail. If there is no strong theoretical argument, they could (for instance) investigate numerically in a tractable setting how close this approximation is.

**Author Response:**

We refer the reviewer to the previous work Ambient Omni (Daras et al NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) Page 9 Theorem 4.2 "Distance contraction under noise", which proves that additive gaussian noise of sufficient variance contracts the TV distance of two arbitrary finite-supported distributions.

---

### Weakness 5: Reproducibility

**Reviewer Comment:**

The paper is not reproducible in the current state. There is no attached code, no detailed description of the implementation and no reproducibility statement. Given that the paper mainly uses empirical arguments of the form "it works better", I consider reproducibility as essential. Also basic information about the required computational resources and the training time is missing.

**Author Response:**

We agree with the reviewer that the paper in its original state did not provide sufficient information to reproduce. To correct this issue, we have since:

1. Made the anonymized code public at https://tinyurl.com/ambientloops
2. Added a reproducibility statement
3. Added extensive information on training hyperparameters, computational resources, and evaluation protocols in Appendix Section D

---

### Weakness 6: Missing Related Work

**Reviewer Comment:**

Literature: The principle of maintaining a dataset and iteratively refine it is often used in the sampling/fine-tuning literature, see e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04468 https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06121 https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.16249 The authors should discuss these works.

**Author Response:**

We thank the reviewer for bringing these important works to our attention. We have cited and discussed these works in the introduction in the revised paper.

---

### Weakness 7: Self-Containment

**Reviewer Comment:**

The paper is not really self-contained. Important parts are "outsourced" to the papers of Daras et al. and reading the submission is not straightforward without reading the references. For instance, the sentence "We study exactly the same problem as Daras et al. (2025c;b;a; 2024)" is not sufficient to define the problem setup. Also, the paper does not really make clear what is already there in those references and what is now new.

**Author Response:**

The reviewer is right that our paper was not sufficiently self-contained. To correct this issue, we have:

1. Explained the experimental setting more fully in Section 5.1 and the new Appendix Section E Noisy dataset formation
2. Added a discussion explaining the relationship and differences to Ambient Omni in more detail in L214

---

### Weakness 3: Efficiency Claims

**Reviewer Comment:**

"Our framework trains to extract as much utility as possible from a given training set; if there is more data available, it is always better to perform training updates on it as fresh samples reveal more about the underlying distribution" has no support sentence on how the method is more efficient than restoring the whole dataset.

**Author Response:**

The Reviewer (most likely) refers to lines 226-231 of our submission. We apologize if the writing is not clear; we are not saying that our method is more computationally efficient. We actually say quite the opposite; our method needs a lot of compute, which is a limitation that we tried to acknowledge.

We rephrased the text to make it more clear (see updated version) and the relevant text below:

> At each round, we have to restore the whole dataset and then fine-tune the model, leading to an increase in the training cost. Indeed, our method is useful when data, not compute, is the bottleneck. If there is more data available, it is always better to use it as fresh samples reveal more about the underlying distribution and there is no need to perform the expensive restoration step that our method requires. However, if there is lack of data, our framework is useful as it attempts to extract as much utility as possible from the given training set.

We hope this clarifies it, and we thank the Reviewer for raising this.

---

### Weakness 4: Paper Exposition for appendix table

**Reviewer Comment:**

Table 5 should be moved to main paper since it is an important evidence.

**Author Response:**

We agree with the Reviewer, this ablation is important. We visualized the results of the Table as a Figure and we added it to our main paper (we also kept the full table in the Appendix). In the main paper, we also expanded the discussion about the findings of this Table. In particular, we emphasized the following takeaways:

- There is an optimal speed when doing multiple loops. Going too slow leads to accumulation of errors and going too fast overestimates the denoising capabilities of the model, leading to learning errors.
- There is a limit to how much the dataset can be denoised. Beyond that limit, models become worse (madness regime, see Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD work).
- Given a fixed computational budget, going fast and performing fewer loops can be optimal.

---

summary.value: This paper proposes Ambient Dataloops, a training strategy to improve diffusion model training in scenarios where datasets are limited but computational resources are available. The method identifies low-quality or out-of-distribution samples in the dataset, corrupts them with parameterized noise levels, and reintroduces them into the training process with estimated noise strengths. This aims to expand the effective training distribution while preserving controllability. Experiments on controlled CIFAR setups, text-to-image generation, and protein design tasks, supported by ablations, demonstrate the effectiveness of Ambient Dataloops.

strengths.value:
- The approach is intuitive and practically motivated, addressing a real challenge in diffusion training when high-quality data is scarce.
- The paper provides theoretical justification explaining why introducing controlled corruption can improve model robustness and training dynamics.
- The empirical evaluation is broad and well-structured, spanning three directions and including ablation studies to demonstrate the contribution of each component.

weaknesses.value: - The real-world evaluation in Section 5.2 is limited to MicroDiffusion. It remains unclear how Ambient Dataloops scale to larger, widely used diffusion models (+ finetuning). For practical adoption, evidence on larger models would be important.

questions.value:
- The controlled CIFAR experiments primarily focus on corruptions of in-domain data. How would explicitly OoD datasets (e.g., SVHN added to CIFAR training) affect the model when used in Ambient Dataloops?
    - Would these samples meaningfully expand the effective data manifold, or would they introduce harmful drift, both in baselines and Ambient Dataloops?
- Ambient Dataloops increase training cost by requiring iterative refinement and reintroduction of samples. How do baseline methods behave when given proportionally increased training compute?
    - Are baselines already near saturation, or could additional training diminish the performance gap?

**Reviewer Comment:**

Several important experimental details are missing (training time, training hyperparameters, diffusion sampling).

**Author Response:**

The Reviewer is right that our paper lacked an analytical discussion of all these hyperparameters. We kept all these hyperparameters fixed from prior work, and hence we omitted discussing them. - Restoration computational requirements (D.3)
- Evaluation Pipeline (D.4)

These sections contain all the necessary information to make our paper reproducible, including analytic tables (Table 7, 8, and 9). We hope that the valid concern of this Reviewer is now addressed.

On top of that, we make all our training code available in the following anonymous URL: https://tinyurl.com/ambientloops

We will de-anonymize the code and make it available to the public upon acceptance of our work. We believe this strongly addressed the concerns of the Reviewer regarding reproducibility.

**Reviewer Comment:**

No confidence intervals or statistical tests are presented in the results tables, so no conclusions about model performance can be drawn.

**Author Response:**

See standard deviations reported above and in the updated tables (Weakness 6 below and the updated Table 1 in the revised paper). That said, to address the Reviewer's concern, we did report all the requested standard deviations that show the statistical significance of our result. We believe that this was a major reason why the Reviewer gave us a low score, and we really hope that this concern is now addressed.

**Reviewer Comment:**

### Weakness 7: Underdeveloped Theory Section

**Reviewer Comment:**

Section 4 on the theoretical framework is very underdeveloped. Lemma 1 is not a lemma since there is no proof. Maybe it is trivial due to prior results, but this should be justified.

**Reviewer Comment:**

Additionally, saying "under appropriate assumptions" without listing those assumptions and proving they are sufficient in the appendix is misleading.

**Author Response:**

We agree with the reviewer that the theory section of our work was not polished. To address this, we added a Lemma 2 in our paper that explicitly states the assumptions for contraction of our posterior sampling scheme. The proof is found in Appendix Section A.

## Questions

### Q1: Source of Protein Metrics

**Reviewer Question:**

It's unclear where the protein metrics came from for baseline models. Did you compute them yourself, or take them from the relevant papers?

**Author Response:**

The protein metrics from the baselines came from the original papers. In particular, we used the numbers from Ambient Protein Diffusion (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight). We have further rerun the metrics ourselves to verify them and we reproduced them successfully.

---

### Q2: Scope of Theoretical Results

**Reviewer Question:**

Do the theoretical results only apply to a single Ambient Loop?

**Author Response:**

Our theory applies to any number of Ambient Loops, as the theory implies the following: suppose that the current diffusion model can sample the distribution p_t, and q_t is some other distribution. Then after a dataloop we will get a distribution that is closer to p_t than q_t. We clarify this in the revised paper, and thank the reviewer for raising this point.

## Summary for the Area Chair

The reviewer had concerns regarding (1) differences to one of our baselines Ambient Omni (2) weakness of Cifar-10 results and lacking a large-scale experiment on ImageNet (3) lacking a justification about efficiency of our method and (4) having an important table in the appendix. We addressed these concerns as follows. For (1) we clarify Ambient Omni used low-quality samples as-is and for a fixed noise times, while Ambient Dataloops improves the low-quality samples and expands the noise times its used for compared to Ambient Omni. For (2) we show how the cifar results actually get us 1/3 of the way to the performance limit of fully uncorrupted data, and that Ambient Dataloops can be used with Flux (12B text-to-image model) to improve the quality of ImageNet while preserving its identity. For (3) we apologize for the confusion and clarify that we are not saying our method is more efficient, but rather the opposite: our method needs a lot of compute, which is a limitation that we tried to acknowledge. For (4) we thank the reviewer and place a new figure visualizing the table in the main paper. The reviewer also had several questions: (1) how to pick the stopping point (2) how to measure data quality improvement (3) what are eligible points and how to sample them and (4) requesting an ablation where only a subset of the low-quality data is improved. We addressed these questions as follows. For (1) the stopping point is chosen empirically using validation metrics. For (2) in CIFAR-10 quality is measured with conditional FID which is typical in the inverse problems literature, and in ImageNet with CLIP-IQA. For (3) eligible points are data points that can be used for a particular diffusion time we want to train with, which are sampled with rejection sampling. For (4) we performed the ablation and added it to the paper.

---

## Weaknesses

### Weakness 1: Difference from Ambient Diffusion Omni

**Reviewer Comment:**

The root of the method is mainly based on AmbientDiffusion. Need to justify on the difference.

**Author Response:**

In Ambient Diffusion Omni, the low-quality parts of the dataset are getting noised to a particular diffusion time, and they can only be used during training for times that correspond to higher noise than the noise level they got mapped to. This is the starting point of our method (loop 0). However, after a successful training, we can now use the model to partially denoise these original noisy points and perform a new training on the resultant dataset.

We added this explanation in the updated version of our paper. We hope this addresses the concern of the Reviewer.

---

summary.value:
The authors propose “Ambient Data Loops”, a method for training diffusion models on a mix of real and noisy data that works by attempting to iteratively denoise the noisy samples. Each step of the loop consists of two components: (1) finetuning on the previous iteration’s data (2) partially denoising the previous iteration’s data. The method builds on prior ambient diffusion works and assumes access to accurate estimates of times $t_i$ for each noisy sample $x_i$ such that training by score matching at $t \in [t_i, T]$ is helpful for $x_i$. In each ambient data loop, the time $t_i$ is halved by using the current model to denoise to time $t_i / 2$ (potentially using multiple samples). 

The algorithm is very roughly theoretically justified without proofs or clearly stated assumptions. In the case that the diffusion model is able to reduce the total variation (TV) distance between the true data distribution and the push-forward of the noisy distribution under denoising, the authors claim the looping procedure will be beneficial. The paper would be stronger if this reduction in TV distance could be theoretically justified.

In Section 5, the authors compare their method to training models that either treat the noisy data as clean (denoted 'No Filtering' in tables) or filter out the noisy data entirely ('Filtering' in tables). Additionally, they compare to ambient diffusion without looping. Results show improvements over No Filtering and Filtering in for both Ambient Diffusion and one Ambient Data Loop. Since there are no confidence intervals and the difference in metrics is small, there is limited evidence that one data loop approves over Ambient Diffusion.

- There are a good number of experiments.

## Questions

### Q1: Dataset Construction Requirements

**Reviewer Question:**

Does the construction of the dataset require to know which images are corrupted and which are not? And do we need to know "how much" they are corrupted? If yes, this seems to be very restrictive to me. How can this be determined if just a dataset is given and we don't know which images are clean and which ones are corrupted how much (which is the most common case in practice)?

**Author Response:**

As mentioned above, our method only requires access to a small set of known high-quality samples. Everything else, including the degradation process and magnitude of all other samples can be estimated; the procedure is described in Appendix Section E Noisy Dataset Formation. Moreover, it is actually impossible for any method (not just ours) to work without this high-quality set. The reason is that if the degradation model is unknown and there is no ground-truth sample access, the underlying distribution of pristine samples is not identifiable.

---

### Q2: Tractable Degradations

**Reviewer Question:**

In their numerics, the authors consider comparibly mild degradations (Gaussian blur, jpeg artifacts). I wondered a bit what kind of degradations can be handled with this method. Are there some which don't work (e.g. what happens with more severe degradations like salt pepper noise/motion blur/contrast changes)? What does a degradation have to fulfill to be tractable?

**Author Response:**

This question is answered in great detail in the work Ambient Diffusion Omni (Daras et al NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight), which our paper builds upon, in Page 6 Section "Learning something from nothing?". To summarize, the method can handle arbitrary corruptions but only works effectively (i.e. significantly better than filtering) in the case of high-frequency corruptions like blur, jpeg compression, and motion blur. In the case of low-frequency corruptions like masking and contrast, the method essentially reduces to filtering.

## Summary for the Area Chair

The Reviewer has concerns about three issues: 1) reproducibility, 2) statistical significance of our results, and 3) rigor of our theory section. From these issues, 1) and 2) were easy to address. In particular, we added very extensive sections on the Appendix about training & sampling hyperparameters and computational times, we open-sourced our code, and we included the standard deviations that the Reviewer required to be convinced of the statistical significance. For 3) Reviewer complained about a lack of proof for a Lemma that we initially omitted due to its simplicity. We have now included the proof of this Lemma, and we have also added another formal Lemma that formalizes the reduction of distance by looping, as requested by the Reviewer.

---

## Weaknesses

### Weakness 1: Theoretical Justification

**Reviewer Comment:**

The algorithm is very roughly theoretically justified without proofs or clearly stated assumptions. In the case that the diffusion model is able to reduce the total variation (TV) distance between the true data distribution and the push-forward of the noisy distribution under denoising, the authors claim the looping procedure will be beneficial. The paper would be stronger if this reduction in TV distance could be theoretically justified.

**Author Response:**

We agree with the reviewer that justifying the reduction would make the paper stronger. In the revised paper, we have added a new Lemma 2 that formalizes the conditions when this occurs, with proof found in Appendix Section A.

#### **Author Response ImageNet:**

The Reviewer further asks for less stylistic and larger-scale experiments on datasets such as ImageNet. To that end, we use the state-of-the-art image-generation model Flux to "restore" ImageNet, i.e., to improve the quality of ImageNet images without compromising the diversity of the dataset. We provide examples from this "improved" ImageNet in Figure 6, and quantitative results in Tables 6 and 7, all found in Appendix Section C of the revised paper.

These examples show that only the quality of the images improved, without altering what is actually depicted in the image. To actually quantify the improvement of quality on ImageNet, we use the CLIP-IQA metric. The results for the original ImageNet and the improved ImageNet are in Tables 6 and 7 in the paper, and also copied below for clarity:

**Table 6: CLIP-IQA Statistics**

| Dataset | Mean ± Std | Min | Max |
|---------|------------|-----|-----|
| Original ImageNet | 0.7251 ± 0.1572 | 0.0184 | 0.9959 |
| Flux-Restored | 0.7469 ± 0.1501 | 0.0265 | 0.9971 |

**Table 7: Pairwise Comparison Winrates**

| Dataset | Winrate Count and % |
|---------|---------------------|
| Original ImageNet wins | 37.82% |
| Flux-Restored wins | 62.17% |

These metrics, paired with our visuals, show that the quality of the dataset improved.

---

## Weaknesses

### Weakness 1: Dataset Construction

**Reviewer Comment:**

The method starts with a dataset of samples, where belongs to the distribution. The paper remains unclear about how to construct this dataset in practice (I noticed that it refers to some literature for this, but for the numerics it should be stated what is done here).

**Author Response:**

The Reviewer is right that our paper lacked an analytical discussion of how the dataset is constructed. We kept the procedure fixed from prior work, chiefly Ambient Omni (Daras et al NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight), and hence we omitted discussing them. That said, the Reviewer is right that the paper needs to be self-sufficient. To that end, we added in the Appendix of our revision the Section E Noisy dataset formation, that explains this process.

---

### Weakness 2: Knowledge of Degradation

**Reviewer Comment:**

The paper often emphasizes that the precise degradation process can be unknown. However, I had the impression that it is required to know which samples are effected by the degradation and how much they are degraded. Correct me if I am wrong, but the paper is not really clear at this point (see also the first question). If this is true, then this has to be clearly addressed in the limitations.

**Author Response:**

The reviewer asks for clarification on the requirements of the algorithm. We clarify that the only thing our algorithm needs is access to a small set of high-quality images. Everything else, including the degradation process and magnitude of all other samples in the dataset can be estimated. As mentioned above, we refer the reviewer to the new Appendix Section E for a full explanation on how this estimation is done. While the knowledge of the high-quality set is a constraint, it is actually impossible for any method (not just ours) to work without it. The reason is that if the degradation model is unknown and there is no ground-truth sample access, the underlying distribution of pristine samples is not identifiable.

---

### Weakness 3: Contractive Nature of OU Process

**Reviewer Comment:**

I am a bit sceptical about the argument that the contractive nature of the OU process really helps. In particular, the reverse of the OU process is an extremely ill-posed problem such that errors in the estimation of the scores will blow up as long as they are not corrected by later score estimates…

**Author Response:**

The reviewer is concerned that using a model-estimated score will lead to errors in the model-restored data. To answer this point, we refer the reviewer to Lemmas 1 and 2 in Section 4 Theoretical Modelling of the main text. In essence, in order for our looping algorithm to succeed we do not need the model restored samples to be perfect, only that they be closer to the true data distribution than the original corrupted (e.g. blurry) distribution. We remark that the model is trained only on clean data or close enough noisy corrupted data (see Appendix Section E and earlier responses). This makes it more intuitive to believe that its outputs will be closer to the true distribution than the strongly corrupted data in the low-quality set $D_l$. Indeed, our algorithm sees the most significant performance gains when going from Loop 0 (Ambient Omni) to Loop 1. As a sanity check, we refer the reviewer to Figure 3 and Table 3 that shows that performing too many subsequent loops eventually does cause learning errors to accumulate and performance to deteriorate.

---

## Summary for the Area Chair

The Reviewer had concerns about presenting only one real-world application with large-scale models, and had questions regarding (1) performance of baselines when given increased training compute equal to Ambient Dataloops and (2) using out-of-distribution data with Ambient Dataloops. We addressed the real-world application concern by adding a new experiment showing how Ambient Dataloops can improve quality while maintaining identity of the ImageNet dataset using Flux (a public 12B text-to-image model), and also by pointing the reviewer to the Proteins experiments which were already in the paper. We addressed the training compute question by clarifying that we always train until saturation for all experiments including baselines, and the out-of-distribution data question by showing how Ambient Dataloops can improve the FID gain from using images of cats to improve a dog generative model.

---

## Reviewer Comments and Author Responses

### Comment 1: Training Compute Comparison

**Reviewer Comment:**

Ambient Dataloops increase training cost by requiring iterative refinement and reintroduction of samples. How do baseline methods behave when given proportionally increased training compute? Are baselines already near saturation, or could additional training diminish the performance gap?

**Author Response:**

This is an excellent question, and we thank the Reviewer for raising this. We updated the paper to clarify it, see the added text below:

> For all of the reported results, we always train the underlying models until performance saturates, and we report from the available checkpoints the one that achieves the best FID. This is to ensure that our method (which requires additional compute compared to the baseline) does not have an unfair advantage. In the experimental settings we study, we are limited by the availability of data, not compute.

---

### Comment 2: Out-of-Distribution Data

**Reviewer Comment:**

The controlled CIFAR experiments primarily focus on corruptions of in-domain data. How would explicitly OoD datasets (e.g., SVHN added to CIFAR training) affect the model when used in Ambient Dataloops? Would these samples meaningfully expand the effective data manifold, or would they introduce harmful drift, both in baselines and Ambient Dataloops?

**Author Response:**

This is another great suggestion. The original Ambient Omni (Daras et al 2025) paper extracted value from OoD datasets by using them for small-diffusion times. The key observation they made is that some datasets (e.g. cats and dogs) are approximately equally distributed locally i.e. have indistinguishable image patches for sufficiently small patch sizes. Thus, training on OoD data in this way expands the effective data manifold, shown through improvements in FID. We report below FID results of training only 10% of the AFHQ dogs dataset (Baseline), adding AFHQ cats (Ambient Omni), and applying Ambient Dataloops. As seen, Ambient Dataloops improves FID compared to Ambient Omni, though the gain is more minor than in the in-domain corruption case as in-domain samples are much more valuable than out-of-domain samples.

| Method | FID |
|--------|-----|
| Baseline (10% dogs) | 12.08 |
| Ambient Omni (10% dogs + 100% cats) | 11.10 |
| Ambient Dataloops (10% dogs + 100% improved cats) | 10.86 |

The datasets suggested by the reviewer, SVHN added to CIFAR, cannot be used as SVHN and CIFAR do not have similar patch distributions: we measured the FID at different patch sizes of two disjoint 25k sample subsets of CIFAR and also one of the CIFAR subsets and a 25k image subset of SVHN. Since the FIDs of the latter pair are much larger, even for patch size 1, we can conclude SVHN cannot be used.

**Patch FID between 25k random CIFAR and 25k disjoint random CIFAR:**

| Patch Size | FID |
|------------|-----|
| 32 | 2.07 |
| 16 | 1.87 |
| 8 | 0.94 |
| 4 | 0.37 |
| 2 | 0.15 |
| 1 | 0.036 |

**Patch FID between 25k random CIFAR and 25k random SVHN:**

| Patch Size | FID |
|------------|-----|
| 32 | 164.34 |
| 16 | 177.86 |
| 8 | 166.69 |
| 4 | 54.76 |
| 2 | 21.58 |
| 1 | 6.95 |

---

## Questions

### Q1: Optimal Stopping Condition

**Reviewer Question:**

What is optimal stopping condition (e.g. L)?

**Author Response:**

Great question! We stop running additional loops when the validation metrics (e.g., test FID) stop improving.

In practice, even a single loop of our method (L=1) leads to improvements. But more loops can further increase performance (see Table 3 and Figure 3).

---

### Q2: Measuring Data Quality Improvement

**Reviewer Question:**

How to measure the gain of data quality improvement?

**Author Response:**

The conditional FID is a metric we use to estimate the data quality improvement, which is typical in the inverse problems literature. We report these results in Table 1, bottom (conditional metrics). For our large-scale experiments that the Reviewer requested, we further use CLIP-IQA as a metric of quality, and we show significant improvements in both the mean score and the win-rate between the original and the improved images (see Tables 6 and 7), which are also validated visually (see Figure 6).

---

### Q3: Eligible Points and Sampling

**Reviewer Question:**

What are eligible points? How to sample it?

**Author Response:**

We assume that the Reviewer refers to the text we had in L5 of Algorithm 1. We apologize for the confusion – we updated the Algorithm to clarify this.

"Eligible" in this context means that the datapoint has a lower noise level than the noise level we want to train for. Simply put, in L5 of the Algorithm, we want to train for a particular noise level $t_{s_i}$, but not all points from the dataset can be used to train at this noise level; if the datapoint has more noise, it is not "eligible" to be used.

We can sample points at random until we find an eligible point (rejection sampling) or sample directly at random only from the pool of eligible points. Our code does the latter, but both implementations are valid.

We hope this comment and the clarification in the paper resolve the confusion of the Reviewer.

---

### Q4: Subset Denoising Ablation

**Reviewer Question:**

Have the authors considered a setting that a subset of denoised dataset is being used compared to a whole? Since this allows to show that quality is over quantity and highlights the essence of data quality.

**Author Response:**

We thank the Reviewer for recommending this experiment. The more high-quality datapoints you have, the better the performance is. Denoising low-quality data points improves the overall as seen from the conditional FID, but can also introduce errors due to having an imperfect model. The ablation suggested by the Reviewer, which we tested by training on a dataset where only 50% of the samples are denoised, obtains slightly better performance than denoising the entire dataset. This suggests 50% of samples are sufficient to learn from the improved dataset while slightly reducing the impact of introduced errors.

| Method | FID |
|--------|-----|
| Ambient Omni (0% restored) | 5.67 |
| Ambient Dataloops (100% restored) | 4.88 |
| Subset Denoising Ablation (50% restored) | 4.85 |
